title: Tree: Inorder Traversal
directAnswer: Inorder = visit Left subtree, then the Node, then the Right subtree. Recursively it's three lines: recurse left, visit, recurse right. The iterative version uses an explicit stack: push all left children, pop-and-visit, then move to the right child of the popped node, and repeat. Both are O(n) time; recursion uses O(h) call-stack space, the iterative version O(h) explicit-stack space. On a BST, inorder yields the values in sorted ascending order.

remember.pattern: Depth-first traversal in Left → Node → Right order
remember.formula:
inorder(node):
    if node is null: return
    inorder(node.left)
    visit(node)
    inorder(node.right)
rules: Order is **Left, Node, Right** — the node is visited *between* its two subtrees.
On a **BST**, inorder prints values in **ascending sorted order** — the signature use case.
Iterative: push left spine, pop-and-visit, then descend into the popped node's right child.
The base case (null → return) is what stops the recursion at the bottom of each branch.
'Inorder' refers to *when the node is visited relative to its children* — middle for inorder, first for preorder, last for postorder.
whenToUse: You need a BST's elements in sorted order without an explicit sort
Validating a BST, finding the kth smallest, or minimum absolute difference
Any traversal where the node belongs logically between its subtrees
antiSignals: You need root-first processing (e.g. cloning, serializing top-down) → preorder
You need children-before-parent (e.g. freeing nodes, computing height) → postorder
You need level-by-level output → BFS level order
remember.takeaway: Inorder is the traversal that 'unrolls' a BST into sorted order. Master both the three-line recursion and the push-left-spine / pop / go-right stack version — the iterative form is the template for Kth Smallest in BST and BST validation.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can produce inorder both recursively and iteratively, and whether you know inorder on a BST yields sorted order.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Mixing up the order (visiting the node before recursing left), or in the iterative version pushing the right child before fully draining the left spine.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Write the recursion instantly, then offer the stack-based iterative version unprompted and connect it to Kth Smallest and Validate BST, which are inorder with extra state.

problemStatement: Given a pointer to the `root` of a binary tree, print the **inorder traversal** of the tree: the values visited in Left-subtree, Node, Right-subtree order, separated by spaces.
constraints: Output values are space-separated in inorder sequence
understanding: Produce the sequence of node values in Left → Node → Right order. For each node we first fully process everything in its left subtree, then the node itself, then everything in its right subtree. On a BST this happens to come out sorted, which is why inorder is the backbone of many BST problems.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should I print the values or return a list?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: HackerRank prints space-separated values. In a general interview, returning a list is cleaner and easier to test — confirm the expected output form.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the tree a BST?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not necessarily. Inorder works on any binary tree; it's just that on a BST the inorder sequence is sorted ascending.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Recursive or iterative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Recursive is the clean default. Offer the explicit-stack iterative version if the interviewer worries about deep recursion or asks to avoid the call stack.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How deep can the tree be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 500 nodes; a skewed tree is 500 deep, which is fine for recursion in Java and Python.

examples.explanation: Left subtree of 4 inorder is 1 2 3, then 4, then right subtree 5. It's a BST, so the output is sorted.
1 has no left child → visit 1, then go right to 2; 2's left is 3 → visit 3, then 2.
Single node — no subtrees, just the node.

diagrams.caption: Inorder visits the node between its subtrees. Compare with preorder (node first) and postorder (node last).

approaches.name: Recursive Inorder — Left, Node, Right
approaches.whenToMention: Start here. Three lines, impossible to get wrong once you fix the order in your head.
hints: Inorder means the node is processed between its two subtrees. In what order do the three actions — recurse left, visit, recurse right — happen?
Write the base case first: a null node produces nothing, so just return.
For a real node: recurse left, then append/print the node's value, then recurse right. That literal translation IS the algorithm.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited exactly once and does O(1) work → O(n) time. The recursion stack is as deep as the tree height h → O(h) space (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed).
approaches.explanation:
Inorder is defined recursively: to traverse a node, fully traverse its left subtree, then visit the node, then fully traverse its right subtree.

**The base case stops the descent.** When recursion reaches a null pointer (the child of a leaf), there's nothing to visit, so it simply returns. This is what unwinds the recursion at the bottom of every branch.

**Why the order matters.** The single line that defines inorder is visiting the node *between* the two recursive calls. Move that visit before the left recursion and you get preorder; move it after the right recursion and you get postorder. The three traversals share identical structure and differ only in where the visit sits.

**The BST payoff.** In a binary search tree every left descendant is smaller and every right descendant is larger. Inorder therefore emits the smallest values first and the largest last — a sorted sequence — without any explicit sorting. That's why Validate BST, Kth Smallest, and Minimum Absolute Difference in a BST all reduce to 'do an inorder and watch the stream'.
approaches.insight: All three DFS traversals are the same three statements — recurse left, visit, recurse right — reordered. Inorder puts the visit in the middle. Anchor on that and you never confuse the three again.

dryRun.intro: Left subtree fully drains before the node, then the right subtree. Output accumulates left to right.

steps.action: 1 is a leaf: left null, visit, right null
back at 2 after its left subtree
back at root after left subtree

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

def inorder(root: Node) -> None:
    if root is None:                   # base case: nothing to visit
        return
    inorder(root.left)                 # 1) left subtree first
    print(root.data, end=' ')          # 2) visit the node
    inorder(root.right)                # 3) right subtree last

java.explanation: Base case — a null child produces no output and unwinds the recursion.
Fully process the LEFT subtree before touching this node.
Visit the node BETWEEN its subtrees — this position is what makes it inorder.

python.explanation: Visit between the two recursions — the inorder position.

diagrams.title: Inorder order on [4,2,5,1,3]
diagrams.caption: Numbers in parentheses show the visit order: 1,2,3,4,5.

edgeCases.behavior: Left null, visit 1, right null → output '1'.
Drills to the deepest left first → output '1 2 3'.

pitfalls: Visiting the node before recursing left — that produces preorder, not inorder.
Forgetting the null base case — infinite recursion / null dereference.
Recursing right before left — reverses the output.

approaches.name: Iterative Inorder — Explicit Stack
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when recursion depth is a concern or the interviewer asks to avoid the call stack. It's also the template for Kth Smallest in BST.
hints: The call stack in the recursive version is really just remembering 'which nodes still need visiting after their left subtree'. Can you keep that memory in an explicit stack?
Maintain a pointer `cur` and a stack. Push every left child as you walk down the left spine until cur is null.
When you can't go left anymore, pop a node, visit it, then set cur to that node's right child and repeat the whole process.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is pushed once and popped once → O(n) time. The stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path of left ancestors → O(h) space.
approaches.explanation:
The recursion's call stack does exactly one thing: it remembers the chain of nodes whose left subtrees we've entered but whose own value we haven't yet printed. We can hold that chain in an explicit stack and reproduce inorder without recursion.

**The two-phase loop.** Keep a current pointer `cur` (start at root) and a stack. Phase one: while `cur` is non-null, push `cur` and move `cur = cur.left` — this walks the left spine, stacking ancestors. When `cur` becomes null we've gone as far left as possible. Phase two: pop a node, visit it (its entire left subtree is already done), then set `cur = popped.right` to explore that node's right subtree. Loop until both the stack is empty and `cur` is null.

**Why visit on pop, not on push.** A node's value may only be emitted *after* its left subtree is fully visited. Pushing records 'I owe this node a visit later'; popping is the moment its left side is finished, so that's when we print and then pivot to its right child.

**Termination.** The loop continues while `cur != null OR stack is non-empty`. The `cur != null` half handles descending into a right subtree that exists even when the stack momentarily empties; the stack half handles backing up to ancestors.
approaches.insight: An explicit stack is just a manual call stack. 'Push the left spine, pop-visit, go right' is the reusable inorder skeleton — bolt on a counter and it becomes Kth Smallest in BST; track the previous value and it becomes Validate BST.

dryRun.intro: Push left spine, pop-visit, then go right. cur tracks where we descend next.

code.python:
def inorder(root: Node) -> None:
    stack = []
    cur = root
    while cur is not None or stack:
        while cur is not None:         # push the entire left spine
            stack.append(cur)
            cur = cur.left
        cur = stack.pop()              # left subtree done -> visit
        print(cur.data, end=' ')
        cur = cur.right                # pivot to the right subtree

java.explanation: Continue while there's a node to descend into OR ancestors still owe a visit.
Walk and stack the left spine until there's no left child.
Pop the deepest unvisited ancestor — its left subtree is fully done.
After visiting, move to the right subtree to repeat the process.

python.line: while cur is not None or stack:
python.explanation: Loop until no node to descend AND no owed ancestors.

python.line: while cur is not None: stack.append(cur); cur = cur.left

python.explanation: Visit on pop — the left subtree finished.

diagrams.title: Stack rising and falling
diagrams.caption: Push the left spine (4,2,1), then pop-visit and pivot right repeatedly.

edgeCases.behavior: Push 1, pop-visit 1, right null, stack empty → '1'.
Each node pushed and immediately popped (no left children) → '1 2 3'.
Whole spine pushed first, then popped in reverse → '1 2 3'.

pitfalls: Visiting on push instead of on pop — emits the node before its left subtree.
Forgetting the `cur != null` half of the loop condition — drops right subtrees that exist when the stack is empty.
Not pivoting to cur.right after the pop — the right subtree is never explored.

commonMistakes: Confusing inorder with preorder by visiting the node before recursing left.
In the iterative version, visiting on push rather than on pop.
Assuming inorder is sorted for ANY tree — it's only sorted for a BST.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong visit position (preorder by accident)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Inorder requires the node to be printed BETWEEN the two recursions. Printing before the left recursion produces preorder output.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Iterative version visits on push
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A node may only be visited after its full left subtree. Printing when you push means the node is emitted before its left descendants.

followupVariations.title: Tree: Preorder Traversal
followupVariations.hint: Same structure; move the visit BEFORE the left recursion (Node, Left, Right).

followupVariations.title: Tree: Postorder Traversal
followupVariations.hint: Move the visit AFTER the right recursion (Left, Right, Node).

followupVariations.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
followupVariations.hint: Iterative inorder, stop after popping the kth node.

followupVariations.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
followupVariations.hint: Inorder must be strictly increasing — track the previous value during the traversal.

patternNote: Inorder DFS (Left → Node → Right). The recursion is one of three traversals that differ only in where the visit sits; the iterative stack version (push left spine, pop-visit, go right) is the reusable template behind Kth Smallest in BST and BST validation. On a BST, inorder is sorted order.
